strengths: Addresses an important question: what multimodal contrastive learning can recover when modalities have distinct, coupled latent variables and private nuisance factors.
Synthetic experiments include known latent factors, three repetitions, and several violations of the assumed distributions.
The proposed feature postprocessing is simple, and reported improvements across multiple CLIP backbones, ImageNet distribution shifts, and 11 few-shot datasets merit further investigation.
weaknesses: The central proof contains a fundamental error. Appendix D.1, Lemma 5.1 claims that the normalized contrastive loss has global minimum zero. Under the paper's spherical vMF model, a matching dot-product score instead gives a normalized population loss of -2I(z_x;z_t), which is negative for dependent latents. For the unit circle with k=tau=1, it is approximately -0.421. Furthermore, condition C1 requires identical embeddings for positive pairs despite full-support conditional noise, forcing constant representations and contradicting C2's uniformity requirement. This invalidates the argument establishing the shared, nuisance-independent encoder used by both identifiability proofs.

The convex-body proof incorrectly treats a limiting statement as an exact identity. In Equation (7), the boundary-dependent conditional normalizer means that uniform p(z_x) generally does not induce uniform p(z_t) at finite lambda. Lemma 4.2 discusses lambda approaching zero, but Equation (43) assumes exact uniformity without this limit. Consequently, Theorem 4.3's cross-entropy reduction is not established. Corollary 4.4 also omits the restriction to L_p metrics with p unequal to 2 used in Appendix E.2; an L2 ball permits arbitrary rotations, contradicting permutation-only identification.

Section 5's FastICA justification is incompatible with the spherical assumptions. Coordinates of a uniformly distributed spherical variable are dependent, and its distribution is rotationally invariant. FastICA therefore cannot resolve its orthogonal mixing into uniquely identifiable latent axes. Counting M-1 intrinsic degrees of freedom does not supply independent Cartesian sources. The alternative PCA argument invokes an unproved local isometry and does not establish the claimed disentanglement guarantee for CLIP.

The experiments do not isolate disentanglement from whitening and dimensionality reduction. Appendix K changes the retained dimensions through FastICA, but provides no matched PCA or whitening controls. At fixed whitening and retained dimension, an orthogonal ICA rotation leaves an L2-regularized linear probe invariant. Thus the reported classification improvements cannot establish an ICA-specific disentanglement benefit.

Actual latent recovery is insufficiently evaluated. CelebA evidence consists of selected decoder traversals and attribute counts, without quantitative disentanglement metrics or controlled comparisons against raw CLIP and PCA. In synthetic experiments, Appendix K regresses learned representations on true latents; a high forward-regression R2 does not establish invertibility or recovery of every latent factor. Downstream accuracy gains cannot validate identifiability of unknown real-world factors.

The causal contribution and novelty are overstated. The undirected edge describes statistical dependence, but its causal semantics and implications for interventions are not formalized. Much of the identifiability machinery explicitly follows Zimmermann et al. [67], making the validity of the new multimodal bridge essential. Its proof failures leave the claimed advance beyond existing representation-identifiability results unsupported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the implementation appendix. Synthetic sample counts and training schedules, the exact data used to fit PCA/FastICA, and component-count selection procedures are unclear. Real-data results lack uncertainty estimates, limiting assessment of stability and the fairness of the few-shot protocol.
